guard: the mapper emits no user-authored text, spends the native callID as the tool identity, and reads a tool part's clock from where a tool part actually keeps it
why: CELLS NAMED BEFORE THE RUN, not selected from the wreckage afterwards.
M1 is the safety property of this connector and the reason the mapping has an authorship arm at
all: OpenCode injects a peer batch by prepending it into the human's own text part, so one record
holds both authors with no boundary in it. Withholding user text is not merely sufficient here as
it is on another connector, it is NECESSARY, because there is no granularity at which the store
M2 is identity. The native callID correlates with the harness, the provider and anything else
reading the same session; a synthesized key correlates only with our own emission. The cell
asserts the native one is spent, and the mutant spends the part id, which is a plausible-looking
identifier that is unique and wrong.
M3 is the bug this build actually had. A tool part keeps its clock on state.time, not part.time,
so reading only part.time arrival-stamps every tool call in a session while a real source stamp
sits one field away. It was caught by measurement, and the cell keeps it caught.

mutations.name: M1 the mapper stops withholding user-authored records
mutations.expectRed: authorship:NO event carries a user part id as its messageId

mutations.name: M2 the tool identity becomes a synthesized key instead of the native callID
mutations.expectRed: tool:toolCallId is the NATIVE callID, not a synthesized key

mutations.name: M3 a tool part's own clock is no longer read, so it falls back to the message's
mutations.expectRed: tool:the source timestamp comes from state.time, where a tool part actually keeps it
